subject: Kids' and teens' slang
title: Teen slang 2026: what does my kid mean? A parent's guide in plain English
answer: Most of what kids say in 2026 comes from TikTok, YouTube and games, and it is usually harmless: "6-7" is a nonsense inside joke, "cooked" means in trouble, "aura" means coolness, "lock in" means focus. Below are the words parents and teachers hear most, what they mean, and the few that are worth a conversation.
body:
6-7 ("six-seven"): a nonsense catchphrase, often shouted with a hand gesture that looks like weighing two things. It comes from the 2025 rap song "Doot Doot (6 7)" by Skrilla and spread through basketball edits about LaMelo Ball, who is 6 feet 7 inches. It has no hidden meaning; even the artist has said he never gave it one. Dictionary.com picked "67" as its 2025 Word of the Year. Example: a teacher says "turn to page 67" and the class erupts.

Aura, aura points, aura farming: aura is how cool someone seems. Doing something embarrassing "loses aura"; "aura farming" is trying a bit too hard to look cool. Example: "He tripped in front of everyone, minus 1,000 aura."

Cooked and cooking: "cooked" means doomed or in trouble ("I didn't study, I'm cooked"), while "cooking" means doing great. Chopped means ugly or bad, and it is not the same as cooked. Lock in means to focus hard ("Finals week, time to lock in"). Crash out means losing your temper or doing something reckless when upset.

Rizz is charm, especially with a crush. Mid means mediocre. Cap means a lie and "no cap" means "for real." Glazing is over-the-top flattery. Ate means did something extremely well ("She ate that presentation"). Delulu, short for delusional, means unrealistic hopes, sometimes said proudly. Unc, short for uncle, teases someone for being old or out of touch. Maxxing means going all in on something, as in "sleepmaxxing." Clanker is an insult for robots and AI, borrowed from Star Wars. Skibidi is a nonsense word from the YouTube animation "Skibidi Toilet"; Cambridge Dictionary added it in 2025. Mogging means outshining someone, usually in looks.

What is worth a conversation: some words come from corners of the internet that are hostile toward women or obsessed with looks. "Sigma" and the "-maxxing" words like "looksmaxxing" grew out of those communities, even if most kids use them as jokes. A few slang terms are crude or sexual; if a word sounds odd, look it up before reacting, and ask your kid where they heard it. Most of the time the honest answer is "a video," and the word will be gone in a few months.

faq.a: It is an inside joke from a 2025 rap song and basketball videos. It has no real meaning, which is part of why kids find it funny.
No. It is a nonsense word from a YouTube animation. Kids use it as a filler or to mean "bad" or "weird" depending on the sentence.

faq.q: What does it mean when my kid says I'm cooked?
faq.a: They mean they are in trouble or doomed, for example before a test they didn't study for.

faq.q: Should I use my kid's slang?
faq.a: Sparingly. Most kids find it funny or embarrassing when parents use it, but asking what a word means is a good way to start a conversation.

faq.q: Which slang words should parents worry about?
faq.a: Words tied to online communities that demean women or push extreme looks culture, and anything sexual or drug-related. If you are unsure, look it up and talk calmly with your child.
